Abdul Azeez vs Food Inspector on 18 January, 2016 Author: B.Sudheendra Kumar Bench: B.Sudheendra Kumar In The High Court Of Kerala At Ernakulam Present: The Honourable Mr. Justice B.Sudheendra Kumar Monday, The 18Th Day Of January 2016/28Th Pousha, 1937 Crl.Rev.Pet.No. 2440 of 2005 ( ) --------------------------------- Crl.A 358/2004 Of The Additional Sessions Court-I, Mavelikkara Cc 1/2000 Of The Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-I, Chengannur Revision Petitioners/Appellants/Accused: ---------------------------------------- 1. Haji B. Abdul Azeez, Nambookavil, Kizhakkethil, Mannar P.O. 2. Fatima Beevi, W/O.Haji B. Abdul Azeez, Nambookavil, Kizhakkethil, Mannar P.O. By Adv. Sri.N.A.Muraleedharan Respondents/Respondents/Complainant & State: ------------------------------------------- 1. Food Inspector, Chengannur Circle. 2. State Of Kerala, Represented By The Public Prosecutor, High Court Of Kerala, Ernakulam. By Public Prosecutor Sri.V.S.Sreejith This Criminal Revision Petition Having Been Finally Heard On 18-01-2016, The Court On The Same Day Passed The Following: Scl. Haji B. Abdul Azeez vs Food Inspector on 18 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/67887601/ 1 B. Sudheendra Kumar, J. ------------------------------------- Crl.R.P. No. 2440 of 2005 -------------------------------------- Dated this the 18th day of January, 2016 Order
texts.facts: The accused in C.C.No.1 of 2000 on the files of the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate-I, Chengannur, filed this revision petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 2 (ia), (j) and 7 (i) r/w Section 16 (1) (a) (ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and Rules 28 and 29 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules. The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:- PW1 , the Food Inspector purchased 750 grams of banana chips on 23.06.1999 at 2.00 p.m. from the first accused. The second accused was the licencee of the said shop. After sampling as per rules, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis. The Public Analyst submitted Ext.P11 report stating that the sample contained synthetic food colour Tartazine and was therefore, adulterated. Thereafter, on the request of the accused, the second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis. Ext .P16 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory also confirmed the presence of synthetic colour Tartazine in violation of Rule 29 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules. It was reported in Ext.P16 that the sample was adulterated. 4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW6 were examined and Exts.P1 to P20 were marked for the prosecution. No evidence was adduced on the side of the revision petitioner.
texts.arguments: 5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext.P16 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument. 6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act. Therefore, Ext. P16 certificate of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra). It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) Haji B. Abdul Azeez vs Food Inspector on 18 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/67887601/ 2 that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal. In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused. The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.
